title: Whatever was rightly said
src: Justin Martyr, Second Apology 13 · tr. Marcus Dods and George Reith (1885)
author: Justin Martyr
translator: Marcus Dods and George Reith (Ante-Nicene Fathers I, 1885)
lines: For each man spoke well in proportion to the share he had of the spermatic word, seeing what was related to it.
Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians.
why: Justin wrote this in Rome about AD 155, a philosopher who had become a Christian and would soon die for it. It is the charter of a whole way of reading: truth is never foreign, wherever you find it, because it comes from the one Word. Say it when you meet something true in an unexpected place.

title: Every good gift
author: James
lines: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above,
coming down from the Father of lights,
with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.
why: The reason Clement and Origen dared to take the gold out of Egypt: if every good gift comes from above, then a true idea is a gift too, whoever found it first. Say it when you are grateful for something good from a source you did not expect.

title: Like the bees
src: Basil of Caesarea, Address to Young Men IV · tr. F. M. Padelford (1902)
author: Basil of Caesarea
work: Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature IV
lines: Now, then, altogether after the manner of bees must we use these writings,
for the bees do not visit all the flowers without discrimination,
nor indeed do they seek to carry away entire those upon which they light,
but rather, having taken so much as is adapted to their needs, they let the rest go.
So we, if wise, shall take from heathen books whatever befits us and is allied to the truth, and shall pass over the rest.
why: Basil's rule for reading, written for his nephews in the fourth century, kept the classics alive in Christian schools for more than a thousand years. Say it before you open a book, a feed or a newspaper: take the honey, leave the rest.
